extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; journalists interested in press origins
extracted.subtask_description: A historical survey of American newspapers and journalism from 1690 to 1940, describing how early colonial presses, formats, distribution, censorship, and news values shaped the development of the U.S. press. The material is aimed at understanding the evolution and social functions of newspapers rather than giving prescriptive modern how-to guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function: correcting false reports / rumor control
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers (and occasional news broadsides) serve to 'prevent false reports' and correct the inevitable abuses of rumor; printing news was recognized as a means 'to prevent false reports.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The broadside The Present State of the New-English Affairs was 'Published to Prevent False Reports.' The text argues that one great function of printing news is to correct abuses of rumor and to supply a faithful relation of events for distant readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship and licensing constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The printing press was 'regarded by government as a dangerous engine' and subject to strict censorship and licensing; free speech and free printing had little legal standing in the colonies at the period's start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples include royal governors instructed to restrain liberty of the press, severe libel laws, and the suppression of Benjamin Harris's Publick Occurrences after one issue. The chapter quotes Sir William Berkeley's opposition to printing and free schools as a governmental fear of dissent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date and serial numbering as markers of a regular newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: A lack of exact date and serial numbering marks a publication as an 'occasional' rather than a regularly issued newspaper; regular serial numbering and dates indicate continuity and periodical status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the undated occasional broadside with later continuous newspapers (e.g., Boston News-Letter) to show how periodicity was signaled to readers and authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values / what made copy 'newsier'
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain topics were privileged as newsworthy: maritime news, arrivals of ships, wars and court affairs, pirate exploits, storms, accidents, and sensational local incidents; human-interest and circumstantial detail increased a paper's 'newsiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: early papers filled two-thirds of space with London political news and the remainder with brief local items; sensational pirate stories (e.g., Blackbeard) were among the most exciting items. The narrative also notes that human-interest stories were relatively rare but valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and physical presentation (page size, columns, leaf count)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers' physical formats—half-sheet single leaves, multi-page issues, page dimensions (e.g., 6 x 9¾ inches)—shaped content and readership; printers used available formats like half-sheets and occasional full sheets with blank pages for correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Publick Occurrences was a three-page 6 x 9¾ inch paper with a blank fourth page; Campbell's News-Letter was a half-sheet usually printed on both sides and sometimes expanded to three or four pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and circulation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: News distribution relied on letters, packets of overseas newspapers brought by ship captains, taverns and coffee-houses maintaining files for patrons, postriders, and later the post office; these channels determined who received news and how fast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The London Gazette and other London papers were imported and read at taverns and coffee-houses; Campbell (postmaster) leveraged his post and postriders to distribute the News-Letter; subscription delivery and packet exchange were central to circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability: subscription pricing and audience size
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper's survival depended on a literate paying audience and sustainable pricing; early papers were often seen as luxuries with limited subscriber bases (e.g., twopence a copy or twelve shillings a year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campbell complained of low vend rates (e.g., 'cannot vend 250 copies'); suspensions occurred when circulation or revenue was inadequate. Presentation (page size, ad space) and content mix affected commercial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of broadsides, pamphlets, and ballads as pre-newspaper media
rubrics_metrics.description: Before regular newspapers, colonists used official proclamations, broadsides, pamphlets, and ballads to disseminate news and commentary; these served many of the functions later taken by newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ballads printed as broadsides celebrated hangings, pirate captures, scandals, and were hawked on the street; broadsides sometimes functioned to correct or proclaim official positions when newspapers were absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for reliable sourcing and skeptical editorial standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The credibility of printed news depended on trustworthy correspondents and verification; the text criticizes faked or fabricated local stories and calls attention to unreliable reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Piscataqua correspondent's capture story was later judged a fiction contrived by a participant; editors who relied on casual or unvetted correspondents risked publishing falsehoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of metropolitan models and content sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Colonial newspapers imitated English papers (especially the London Gazette), borrowing formats, editorial approaches, and a large share of content from London journals; metropolitan content often dominated colonial issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The News-Letter filled about two-thirds of its space with news taken from London journals (English politics, court, European wars) and filled remaining space with brief local items. This imitation shaped early colonial news agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and role of advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements appeared in limited, often subordinate positions (e.g., bottom of the last column) and formed a modest but essential revenue source in early issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early issues usually included a few advertisements; their size and placement reflected production constraints and the paper's economic model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial caution regarding seditious or high reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors risked suppression and punishment for publishing 'reflections of a very high nature' or seditious material; cautious editorial practices and licensing were used to avoid governmental retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benjamin Harris's Publick Occurrences was suppressed after the Governor objected to reflections on foreign monarchs and reports judged 'doubtful and uncertain.' The book recounts how colonial authorities forbade publication without license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press as a popular institution and political force
rubrics_metrics.description: Because printing sells to large numbers, the press functioned as a popular institution and a constant threat to governmental control; its political power and social reach made it a focus of regulation and contestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative emphasizes government mistrust of popular interference and shows how both governors and colonial assemblies tried to control printing while also using it for official purposes.
